rationale: A wins because it keeps the founder closer to what a reporter can actually prove. "Half a million secondhand Patagonia items later, the company still won't say if resale pays" names a real disclosure gap, then demands the denominator instead of decorating the stat. B has useful bones, but "triages it into free/at-cost/resale" invents plumbing the update never gave us, and "Only a company with no shareholders to please" turns a plausible governance question into an overclaim.
gaps_in_A: "A company with no shareholders is giving away repairs — nobody else can copy the math" overstates the update. Privately held and profit-directed is not the same as no shareholders, and "nobody else" is lawyer-bait without competitor proof.
"Story type: category-creation" is inflated. This is a retail-operations or reverse-logistics rollout unless Patagonia can show it is creating a category, not just expanding a service.
A underplays the separate business-model tension B spots: free repairs plus no new apparel line can be framed against replacement-cycle apparel retail without making the whole story about ownership.
gaps_in_B: "triages it into free/at-cost/resale" is invented. The update says repair and Worn Wear resale both exist; it does not say mailed or dropped-off items route into resale.
"Only a company with no shareholders to please could give repairs away" is too confident. The supplied facts support a governance question, not that sweeping conclusion.

"The prevailing model in apparel is volume" may be true, but it is imported context, not supplied evidence. Before pitching that contrarian angle, it needs a source or a reporter will make you earn it the hard way.
"journalist-fit-check — four viable shapes exist" is premature. The sharper next move is to test novelty and prior Worn Wear coverage before burning reporter names on an incremental rollout.
